LEARNING OBJECTIVES: Define data product design; explain its mechanism; apply it to a realistic problem; measure or evaluate the result; identify assumptions, limitations, failure modes, security or governance implications, and connections to prior lessons.

CONCEPT: Data Product Design is taught as a progressively applied competency. Identify the objective, inputs, mechanism, outputs, constraints, and evidence. Distinguish established facts from inference and forecasts. At higher levels, compare alternative methods and justify the selected approach.

METHOD: Define the problem -> establish a baseline -> gather reliable inputs -> apply the method -> calculate or observe the result -> test assumptions -> compare alternatives -> document limitations -> measure the real outcome -> revise.

WORKED APPLICATION: A small organization faces a decision involving data product design. The learner constructs a baseline, identifies the variables that matter, chooses a method consistent with the evidence, and records both expected and actual outcomes. Where computation is relevant, show the formula, algorithm, query, or system flow rather than reporting an unexplained answer.

PRACTICE: Solve one guided example, then an independent scenario with changed assumptions. State what evidence would falsify the conclusion. Identify at least one downstream effect on business, finance, customers, technology, security, or operations.

AI/TOOLS: Use appropriate calculators, spreadsheets, code, analytics, or AI assistance when they improve learning or execution. Validate generated claims and calculations. Never treat AI output as primary evidence merely because it is fluent.

FAILURE MODES: undefined objective; poor source data; hidden assumptions; inappropriate method; correlation/causation confusion; false precision; metric gaming; ignored exceptions; unsafe permissions; automation without monitoring.

MASTERY: Explain the concept without prompts, execute it on a novel example, interpret the result, diagnose an error, and connect it to the next level of the subject.
